title: The monastery hospitals of Sri Lanka

traditional.note: The *Mahavamsa* chronicle credits King Pandukabhaya, who by its reckoning reigned in the 4th century BCE, with a lying-in house and a hall for the sick.

confidence.note: Excavation and the ground plan identify the Mihintale ruins as a monastic hospital; archaeological descriptions date it to the 9th century, though a site sign at Polonnaruwa calls it an 8th-century prototype. The far earlier royal hospitals rest only on a chronicle composed around 500 CE.

people: Pandukabhaya (4th century BCE by the chronicle's reckoning), king credited by tradition with the island's first hospitals
summary: A Buddhist hospital with cells for patients and a stone trough for medicinal baths — and a chronicle claiming hospitals 1,200 years older.
body: On the sacred hill of Mihintale, near Sri Lanka's ancient capital Anuradhapura, excavators uncovered a monastery hospital: rows of separate cells for patients and a large stone trough used as a medicinal bath, for a community of perhaps 2,000 monks. The ruins date from around the 9th century, and the design was copied at a 12th-century hospital in Polonnaruwa, where patients were immersed in herbal oil. The chronicle known as the *Mahavamsa* claims far more: that King Pandukabhaya built a lying-in house and a hall for the sick in the 4th century BCE. But it was composed around 500 CE, centuries later.

myth.tradition: Sri Lanka had public hospitals in the 4th century BCE, and Mihintale is the oldest hospital in the world.
myth.record: The 4th-century BCE hospitals are known only from the *Mahavamsa*, written about 900 years later. The Mihintale ruins themselves date from roughly the 8th–9th century CE.

links.note: An earlier Buddhist ruler's claim to have provided medical care.
The Christian charitable hospital, a parallel religious tradition.

title: The Four Tantras of Tibetan medicine

traditional.note: Tradition holds that the Buddha, as the Medicine Buddha, taught the text, and links its arrival in Tibet to an 8th-century physician, Yuthok the Elder.

confidence.note: Museum and scholarly sources credit the text to the 12th-century physician Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger, and scholars place the formation of the tradition between the 7th and 12th centuries. The earlier history of the text, and how much of it he composed rather than edited, is debated; the Buddha's authorship is religious tradition.

people: Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger (1127–1203), physician credited with the text
summary: One book underlies the medicine of Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan and the Himalaya — and tradition says the Buddha himself dictated it.
body: The *rGyud bzhi*, or Four Tantras, is the single standard treatise on which Tibetan medicine rests, together with its Mongolian, Bhutanese and Himalayan offshoots. The tradition it codified took shape in Central Tibet between the 7th and 12th centuries out of Tibetan, Indian, Chinese, Persian and Central Asian medical knowledge. The text is credited to the physician Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger (1127–1203), honored as Tibet's physician king. Tradition tells a grander story, shown in paintings: one sage asks the Medicine Buddha to explain the Four Tantras and another recites the answers, which is why the book is written as questions and answers.

myth.tradition: The Four Tantras are the Buddha's own teaching, carried to Tibet in the 8th century and handed down unchanged.
myth.record: This is religious tradition. Historians credit the text to Yuthok the Younger in the 12th century and trace its contents to several medical traditions; an 8th-century Yuthok the Elder is regarded as legendary.

links.note: Indian Ayurvedic learning was one of the sources Tibetan medicine drew on.

title: Greco-Arabic medicine takes root in India

confidence.note: This was a slow transplantation rather than an event; Sultan Firuz Shah's own account documents a physician-staffed hospital in 14th-century Delhi. Later details, such as when the name *Unani* came into use, come from secondary accounts.

place: Delhi and other Muslim courts of northern India
people: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (born 1309), sultan of Delhi who endowed a hospital
Hakim Ajmal Khan, Delhi physician and founder of the Tibbia College
summary: A sultan's free hospital in Delhi, Persian doctors at the Mughal court, and a Greek-rooted medicine that is still taught across India.
body: Greek medicine, recast in Arabic and Persian, reached India with its Muslim rulers. At the Delhi Sultanate and the later Muslim courts, its physicians practiced *tibb* alongside Ayurvedic colleagues and borrowed Indian drugs. In the 14th century Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq recorded that he endowed a hospital where physicians diagnosed the sick, regulated their diet and gave medicines at his expense, to "residents and travelers, gentle and simple, bond and free." Only in the late 18th century did the tradition take the name *Unani*, "Greek." It outlasted British rule: Hakim Ajmal Khan's Tibbia College in Delhi taught it outside the colonial system, and it remains a state-recognized medicine today.

links.note: Avicenna's *Canon* was the core text carried to Indian courts.
The Islamic endowed hospital that Delhi's sultans copied.

title: Smallpox inoculation in Bengal

confidence.note: Holwell's printed account is firmly dated to 1767, and a Bengal vaccination official confirmed its outline in 1805. How long Bengalis had inoculated before that is undocumented.

people: J. Z. Holwell, Fellow of the Royal Society, author of the 1767 account
summary: Traveling Brahmin inoculators, a smallpox goddess and a strict diet: Bengal's way of beating smallpox as reported to London in 1767.
body: In 1767 J. Z. Holwell told London's College of Physicians how Bengal protected itself against smallpox. Every year, he wrote, small parties of Brahmin inoculators set out from religious centers such as Benares to reach the villages before the smallpox season. Patients were prepared with a diet free of fish, milk and ghee; after inoculation, cold water was poured over their heads and offerings made to Sitala, goddess of smallpox. A vaccination official found the account still broadly true in 1805. Holwell claimed the practice had "the sanction of remotest antiquity," but nobody has shown how old it was.

myth.tradition: Indian inoculation, or even vaccination itself, goes back thousands of years and is described in ancient Sanskrit texts.
myth.record: The age of Bengali inoculation is undocumented; colonial writers' 'time immemorial' was a stock phrase for customs of unknown origin. The supposed ancient Sanskrit account of vaccination first appeared in the *Madras Courier* in 1819 and may have been deliberate propaganda.

links.note: The Ottoman route by which inoculation reached England.
Vaccination later displaced inoculation in India, against resistance.

title: An Indian nose job astonishes London

confidence.note: The *Gentleman's Magazine* letter of October 1794 survives and was reprinted by Carpue in 1816. Sources differ slightly on when the operation itself took place (1793 or after a year without a nose following capture in 1792), and the operator is never named.

place: Near Poona (Pune), India; reported in London
people: Cowasjee, bullock driver with the British army and the patient
Thomas Cruso and James Findlay, Bombay surgeons who witnessed the operation
Joseph Constantine Carpue (1764–1846), London surgeon who adopted the method
summary: A mutilated bullock driver, a new nose cut from his forehead by a nameless craftsman near Poona, and a letter that revived plastic surgery in Europe.
body: In October 1794 London's *Gentleman's Magazine* printed a letter, signed only "B. L.," about a man named Cowasjee. A bullock driver with the British army in the war of 1792 against Tipu Sultan of Mysore, he had been taken prisoner and had his nose and one hand cut off. After more than a year without a nose he was given a new one by "a Mahratta surgeon, a Kumar" near Poona, while two Bombay surgeons, Thomas Cruso and James Findlay, watched.

A wax model of a nose was flattened and traced on the forehead. The skin was cut free except for a narrow bridge between the eyes, which kept its blood supply, then turned down and fixed to the stump. The letter said the operation was "not uncommon in India." Engravings of Cowasjee were published in London.

Europe had once had its own flap operations, from 16th-century Italy, but they had fallen out of use. In London, Joseph Constantine Carpue studied the reports, practiced on cadavers and in 1814 rebuilt an officer's nose; his 1816 book spread what became known as the Indian method. The Indian surgeon's name was never recorded.

myth.tradition: The Poona surgeon was performing Sushruta's ancient operation, handed down unchanged for two thousand years.
myth.record: The *Sushruta Samhita* describes a flap cut from the cheek, not the forehead. Nasal repair clearly had a long history in India, but how the 18th-century forehead method descended from the ancient text is undocumented.

links.note: The ancient Sanskrit text that describes nasal reconstruction with a cheek flap.

title: From sarpagandha to reserpine

confidence.note: CIBA's 1952 isolation and launch of reserpine are well documented. Accounts differ on minor points, such as who first isolated the alkaloid and in which year, and on how far back the root's medical use can be traced.

place: Calcutta and Bombay, India; Basel, Switzerland
people: Gananath Sen, Calcutta physician trained in Ayurveda
summary: A root sold in Indian bazaars to calm the insane became, via Calcutta doctors and a Swiss firm, a blood-pressure pill and an early drug for psychosis.
body: The root of *Rauwolfia serpentina*, sarpagandha, was sold across India above all as a remedy for insanity. In 1931 two Calcutta physicians, Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose, reported that 20 to 30 grains of the powder twice daily calmed violent patients and lowered blood pressure. After Rustom Jal Vakil's 1949 paper in the *British Heart Journal*, the Swiss firm CIBA isolated the active alkaloid, reserpine, in 1952 and sold it as Serpasil for high blood pressure. Nathan Kline then showed it worked in psychosis, and in 1957 he and Vakil shared Lasker honors with chlorpromazine's pioneers.

myth.tradition: Reserpine is an ancient Ayurvedic drug, recorded in Indian texts for some 3,000 years.
myth.record: The root was widely used in Indian folk and bazaar medicine, but Bose wrote in 1932 that no drug matching it could be found in the classical Ayurvedic lexicons, and called the 'Ayurvedic' names misnomers.

links.note: The other early antipsychotic, honored alongside reserpine in 1957.
Unani physicians such as Hakim Ajmal Khan also prescribed the root.
